disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops following exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, through learning of it happening to a close other, or via repeated exposure to aversive details. It is characterized by persistent re-experiencing of the trauma, avoidance of reminders, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked changes in arousal and reactivity lasting more than one month and causing functional impairment. The clinical course can be acute or chronic, with onset sometimes delayed, and is often complicated by comorbid depression, anxiety, or substance use. PTSD is distinguished from other anxiety and mood disorders by the requirement of a qualifying traumatic event and the specific pattern of trauma-linked intrusions, avoidance, and hyperarousal.

narrative.stressor: About two years ago, Regino was overseeing a night shift at the industrial equipment plant when a malfunctioning press catastrophically failed, severely injuring one longtime employee and killing another he had mentored for years. As plant manager, he was the one who had signed off on the maintenance schedule and then had to coordinate emergency response, give statements to OSHA and corporate investigators, and face the deceased worker’s family at the funeral, all while trying to keep the facility running and protect his team’s jobs. In the months that followed, corporate pressure to restore production, ongoing legal reviews, and his own perfectionistic sense of responsibility kept him locked into long hours, cutting into his fishing, church volunteering, and family barbecues that once grounded him. Around the 10–12 month mark, his wife and coworkers noticed that he was no longer able to function like the meticulous, steady leader they knew—he started avoiding certain parts of the plant, resisted travel for regional meetings, and his performance review flagged concerns about his concentration and temperament—leading the company’s EAP and his parish priest to both urge him to seek psychiatric help.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since the accident at the plant, I feel like I’m constantly on edge and scanning for something to go wrong, even when I’m just at home.”

narrative.stressor: A little under two years ago, Chanelle was closing up a retail location she was consulting for when an armed robbery occurred; she was forced at gunpoint to lie on the floor while one of the younger employees was pistol-whipped nearby, and she genuinely believed someone was going to be killed. In the aftermath, she threw herself into supporting the staff, giving statements to police, and designing new safety protocols, while privately trying to keep up her usual commitments to mentoring, salsa class, and church activities as if nothing had changed. Over the following year, she started quietly avoiding evening events in the neighborhood where the robbery took place, became more reluctant to drive alone at night, and found that her enjoyment of museum visits and jazz concerts was increasingly overshadowed by a sense of dread in crowded or unfamiliar spaces, which began to interfere with her work travel and community leadership roles. When she turned down a speaking invitation for a women’s leadership conference because it was scheduled for an evening in a downtown venue and realized she was arranging her life around not feeling safe, she discussed it with a close friend from her business network, who suggested she see a psychiatrist through her primary care clinic.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since that robbery, I keep organizing my whole life around avoiding anything that reminds me of it—certain neighborhoods, late meetings, even some community events.”

narrative.stressor: Approximately one year and seven months ago, Jesse was driving his wife home from a medical appointment when another car ran a red light and slammed into the passenger side, leaving her trapped and badly injured while he was stuck in the driver’s seat, unable to reach her until first responders arrived. In the weeks that followed, he split his time between his own physical recovery and spending long days at the hospital and rehab facility, taking on the role of primary caregiver and household manager while trying to maintain his volunteer work and gardening routines. As his wife slowly improved, he found it progressively harder to resume his usual activities—he stopped taking longer drives to historic sites, became reluctant to venture beyond familiar local roads, and his meticulous planning for trips and community events dwindled as even short car rides felt overwhelming and exhausting. When his daughter noticed he had started avoiding driving altogether, canceling library volunteer shifts and declining to attend a grandchild’s school play because it involved a highway route, she accompanied him to his primary care doctor, who referred him for a psychiatric evaluation after recognizing the persistent trauma-related impact on his daily functioning.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since the crash, even small things on the road make me jump out of my skin, and I can’t bring myself to drive like I used to.”
